Print a gtable object as a tibble

Source: R/gtable-print.R
gtable_print.Rd

Prints a gtable object in an easier-to-read format compared to the default gtable print method. There are also extra options for conveniently subsetting the printed gtable.

Usage

gtable_print(x, zsort = FALSE, show_zeroGrobs = TRUE, filter = NULL)

Arguments

x

A gtable object, or an object coercible to a gtable, like a ggplot or patchwork object.

zsort

Sort by z values? Default FALSE.

show_zeroGrobs

TRUE/FALSE for whether to show zeroGrobs.

filter

If a character vector of regexes, only grob names matching at least one regex will be printed. If NULL (the default), no filtering by grob name.

Details

gtable_print() prints a gtable's layout using a custom tibble subclass, allowing for some parts of a standard printed tibble to be hidden, like the "# A tibble..." header line and the row of column types.

The cells column in the output is slightly different than the cells column in the default gtable print method. Specifically, gtable_print() simplifies cells in cases where a grob sits in only one row or one column. E.g., if a grob is just in row 3 and column 2, then the default method would print "(3-3, 2-2)", while gtable_print() prints "(3, 2)".

See also

gtable_show_grobs()

Examples

# Let's print the gtable of a ggplot object. For comparison we'll use both
# the default method and gtable_print().
library(ggplot2)
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(hp, mpg))

# Convert p to a gtable and print with the default printing method. Note that
# the "grob" column may get separated from the rest of the table, depending
# on the console width. That makes it hard to read.
gtable::as.gtable(p)
#> TableGrob (16 x 13) "layout": 22 grobs
#>     z         cells             name
#> 1   0 ( 1-16, 1-13)       background
#> 2   5 ( 8- 8, 6- 6)           spacer

#> 7   9 (10-10, 7- 7)           axis-b

#> 9   8 ( 9- 9, 8- 8)           axis-r
#> 10  2 (10-10, 8- 8)           spacer
#> 11 10 ( 7- 7, 7- 7)           xlab-t
#> 12 11 (11-11, 7- 7)           xlab-b
#> 13 12 ( 9- 9, 5- 5)           ylab-l

#> 21 20 ( 3- 3, 7- 7)            title
#> 22 21 (14-14, 7- 7)          caption

#> 2                                zeroGrob[NULL]
#> 3            absoluteGrob[GRID.absoluteGrob.25]

#> 5                                zeroGrob[NULL]
#> 6                       gTree[panel-1.gTree.16]
#> 7            absoluteGrob[GRID.absoluteGrob.21]
#> 8                                zeroGrob[NULL]
#> 9                                zeroGrob[NULL]
#> 10                               zeroGrob[NULL]
#> 11                               zeroGrob[NULL]

#> 13   titleGrob[axis.title.y.left..titleGrob.32]

#> 15                               zeroGrob[NULL]
#> 16                               zeroGrob[NULL]

# Better printing with gtable_print() -- the columns all stay together, with
# wide columns (e.g., "grob") getting abbreviated if needed. Note that
# gtable_print() handles the conversion of p to a gtable automatically.
gtable_print(p)
#> TableGrob (16 x 13) "layout": 22 grobs
